question_text: A 43-year-old gentleman with a history of intravenous drug use presents with general fatigue and weakness accompanied by swelling in his ankles and lower legs. Further questions elicit that he has had many infections due to his drug use but has not previously had any cardiac or pulmonary issues. Upon physical examination you notice a holosystolic blowing murmur radiating to the right sternal border, which the patient denies being told about previously. Based on this presentation, what is the most likely cause of the murmur?

        ### Question
        A 43-year-old gentleman with a history of intravenous drug use presents with general fatigue and weakness accompanied by swelling in his ankles and lower legs. Further questions elicit that he has had many infections due to his drug use but has not previously had any cardiac or pulmonary issues. Upon physical examination you notice a holosystolic blowing murmur radiating to the right sternal border, which the patient denies being told about previously. Based on this presentation, what is the most likely cause of the murmur?

        ### Options
        opa. Ventricular septal defect
opb. Tricuspid stenosis
opc. Tricuspid regurgitation
opd. Mitral stenosis
ope. Mitral regurgitation

### Reasoning Chains per Option:
CHAIN: Intravenous drug use -> increased risk of infective endocarditis -> valvular damage -> heart murmur -> 80% CHAIN: Holosystolic blowing murmur radiating to the right sternal border -> indicative of tricuspid regurgitation -> 90% CHAIN: Swelling in ankles and lower legs -> suggestive of right-sided heart failure -> tricuspid regurgitation -> 80%

### Retrieved Evidence Paths (broad but correct):
